title: SQL vs NoSQL
subtitle: Watch one online shop send each kind of data to the store whose shape fits its access pattern.
learn: How relational tables, schemas and joins let you ask questions you did not plan for
What key-value, document, wide-column and graph stores each optimize
Why NoSQL stores usually require you to design around known queries
How to choose a store by access pattern instead of by hype
Why most systems start with one relational database and add others only when forced

steps.title: One shop, five kinds of data
steps.body: An online shop stores five kinds of data: orders, login sessions, a product catalog, click events, and a 'people also bought' network. Each kind is written and read in a different way. Should they all share one database, or should each get its own? The numbers in this lesson are rough single-server figures that show scale, not benchmarks.
steps.idea: Pick a database by how the data is read and written, not by whether it is called SQL or NoSQL.
steps.caption: The shop app has five kinds of data and five possible stores.

steps.title: Orders in tables with a schema
steps.body: Watch checkout. The app sends one transaction (a group of writes that all succeed or all fail) to a relational (SQL) database. It keeps data in tables of rows and columns, like linked spreadsheets: customers, orders, order_items. The schema (the declared columns and types) is a contract the database enforces, including foreign keys (a column that must point at a real row in another table). Three tables are written, then COMMIT confirms all three at once. A well-tuned PostgreSQL server handles thousands of such writes per second (8,000 here).
steps.idea: A relational schema trades flexibility for guarantees: the database itself rejects bad or half-written data.
steps.caption: Checkout: one transaction writes three tables, then the database replies COMMIT ok.

steps.title: Ask a question nobody planned for
steps.body: Next quarter someone asks: what is the revenue per product category for customers who signed up in Berlin? Relational data is normalized, meaning each fact is stored once in its own table. So one SQL query can join (link up rows from) customers, orders, items and products to answer it. Nobody had to predict this question when the tables were designed. With indexes, a shop-sized dataset answers in about 800 ms. Heavy reports like this usually move to a replica or warehouse, covered later.
steps.idea: Normalized tables plus joins let you answer new questions without changing how the data is stored.
steps.caption: One query joins four tables on demand and returns the totals.

steps.title: Sessions: give me the value for this key
steps.body: A login session is read on every request, and only ever by its session id. A key-value store such as Redis maps a key to a value and is built for exactly that lookup. There are no joins or ad hoc queries, and Redis keeps data in memory. So the app's GET returns in about 0.5 ms, and one node serves 100,000 or more operations per second. Disk-based stores like DynamoDB take a few milliseconds. An in-memory store needs persistence or replication if sessions must survive a restart.
steps.idea: A key-value store is the fastest design when the only question is 'what is stored under this key?'
steps.caption: The app asks for one session id and gets the session back in 0.5 ms.

steps.title: Catalog: one product, one document
steps.body: A laptop has RAM and ports; a T-shirt has size and fabric. Forcing both into one table leaves many empty columns or needs many joined tables. A document store such as MongoDB keeps each product as one JSON-like document with whatever fields it needs, so one read returns the whole product page (2 ms here). The cost: by default your code, not the database, enforces the shape (some stores offer optional validation), and joins across documents are limited and often slower at scale.
steps.idea: Documents fit data that is read and written as one self-contained unit with varying fields.
steps.caption: One lookup by SKU returns the whole product document.

steps.title: Click events: huge write volume
steps.body: During a sale the shop logs 200,000 click events per second. Spread over a 5-node cluster, each node takes about 40,000 writes per second. A wide-column store such as Cassandra or ScyllaDB splits data by a partition key (say user id) and sorts rows inside each partition by a clustering key such as time. Writes are cheap appends. 'Latest 50 events for user 42' reads one sorted slice from one partition. The catch: you design each table around a known query, and other queries are slow. These stores often favor availability, so reads can be slightly stale (see Replication).
steps.idea: Wide-column stores scale writes by making every query hit one partition, so you design the table around the query.
steps.caption: The app appends clicks, then reads one sorted slice for user 42.

steps.title: Recommendations: follow the relationships
steps.body: 'Customers who bought this also bought...' means walking from a product to its buyers, then to their other purchases: two or three hops. In SQL each hop is another join (here a self-join, a table joined to itself). With indexes, two or three hops are fine, but results multiply and deep or variable-length paths get slow and awkward. Many graph databases store each node's neighbours directly, so a walk costs about the number of links visited (5 ms here), not the table sizes. Real recommenders often precompute results, so graphs earn their place when live path queries are the product.
steps.idea: Pick a graph store when queries are about paths and neighbours several hops deep.
steps.caption: The app asks for items 2-3 hops away and the graph follows stored links.

steps.title: Run the finance report on the document store
steps.body: Suppose orders had gone into the document store because it was fashionable. The revenue-by-category question now needs data from three collections. A document store can join (MongoDB has $lookup), but its joins are limited and are not what the model is built for. So you either combine orders, products and customers in application code, or you copy product and customer fields into every order. Here the app fetches a quarter of orders and joins them in code, which takes about 3 seconds. Copied fields must then be kept in sync.
steps.idea: NoSQL stores make known queries fast by pre-shaping data; unplanned queries then cost you code or copies.
steps.caption: The app pulls three collections and joins them itself, which takes seconds.

steps.title: Start boring, add stores on evidence
steps.body: A common mistake is adopting five databases on day one. As a rule of thumb, one relational database with good indexes and read replicas handles most products well past a million users, and it gives you transactions, constraints and joins. Add a key-value cache when reads hurt: the app checks the cache first, reads SQL only on a miss, then fills the cache so later reads take 0.5 ms. Add wide-column or time-series storage when writes outgrow one node, and a graph store when traversals dominate. Each extra store is more to run, and cached copies can go stale, so decide when they expire.
steps.idea: Every extra database is one more thing to run, back up and keep in sync, so add one only for a measured need.
steps.caption: Cache miss: the app reads SQL, then fills the cache. Later reads hit it at 0.5 ms.

steps.title: Choose by access pattern
steps.body: Relational suits structured data, joins and transactions, and can answer questions nobody planned. Key-value is fastest for lookups by key. Documents suit self-contained records with varying fields. Wide-column scales heavy writes when queries are known and fit one partition. Graphs suit deep relationship queries. Ask how the data is read and written, how consistent it must be, and how big it gets. The lines blur: Postgres stores JSON in JSONB columns, and MongoDB offers multi-document transactions. So choose by access pattern, not by label.
steps.idea: List your queries first; the store that serves them directly is usually the right one.
steps.caption: Each store matches one access pattern.

quiz.q: Your team must answer a brand-new analytics question tomorrow that combines customers, orders and products, and nobody planned for it. Which design makes that easiest?
options: A key-value store keyed by order id
Normalized relational tables queried with joins
A wide-column table designed for the click-event query
Denormalized documents with product data copied into each order
quiz.why: Normalized tables store each fact once, so joins can combine them in ways nobody anticipated. The other designs were shaped around specific known queries.

quiz.q: A service only ever fetches a user's session blob by session id, millions of times per second. What is the best fit?
options: A graph database
A relational database with many joins
A document store with secondary indexes on every field
A key-value store
quiz.why: The only access pattern is lookup by key, which is exactly what key-value stores optimize, with no query planner or joins to pay for.

quiz.q: In a wide-column store you need to list a user's latest events, and later also list all events from one country. Why is the second query a problem?
options: The table is partitioned by user, so a country query would scan every partition unless you add a second table laid out by country
Wide-column stores cannot store country values at all, because columns must be declared up front for every row
Country lookups require a graph traversal, because a wide-column store cannot follow relationships otherwise
Wide-column stores only support writes, so every read has to go through a separate search engine
quiz.why: Data is placed by partition key and efficient queries must supply it. A different query needs a differently keyed copy of the data.

quiz.q: Which statement about 'NoSQL scales, SQL does not' is most accurate?
options: It is true for writes only, because SQL databases serialize all writes on one machine
It is false: NoSQL stores are slower than SQL on every workload, so they never scale better
It oversimplifies: NoSQL stores often scale out by limiting query types, while a single SQL node already handles very large workloads
It is true because NoSQL stores never need indexes and so avoid the overhead that limits SQL
quiz.why: Scale-out comes mostly from restricting queries to one partition, not from the data model's label. One relational node often serves many products, and databases that spread SQL across many nodes also exist.

quiz.q: You store each order as a document that embeds a copy of the product name and price. A product is renamed. What is the main consequence?
options: Old orders automatically update, because the store tracks references to the product
Order reads become slower, because each document must be rewritten on every read
The document store rejects the rename until every order embedding the old name is migrated
Existing orders keep the old copy, so you decide whether to leave or update them
quiz.why: Embedding duplicates data for fast single-read access. Sometimes keeping the price paid at purchase time is desired, but other copies need explicit synchronization.

cheatsheet.def: The declared structure of data. SQL enforces it on write; many NoSQL stores leave it to application code by default (schema-on-read, meaning the shape is interpreted when data is read), though some offer optional validation.
Storing each fact once across related tables to avoid duplication. Joins reassemble the data at query time.
Copying data into the place it is read to avoid joins. Reads get faster; writes must keep copies in sync.
Maps a key to a value and is optimized for lookup by key; no joins or ad hoc queries (some stores add data structures or sort keys). Examples: Redis, DynamoDB.

Stores self-contained JSON-like records with flexible fields. Good for read-as-a-unit data such as catalogs. Joins across collections exist (MongoDB $lookup) but are limited compared with a relational engine's joins. Example: MongoDB.
Partitions rows by a key and sorts them within the partition. Built for heavy writes and known queries. Examples: Cassandra, ScyllaDB.
Stores nodes and edges and traverses relationships directly. Best for multi-hop questions like recommendations or fraud rings.
Write down your top queries and consistency needs first. Default to relational; add a specialized store only for a measured mismatch.
